subject: redPanda
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: red panda balancing on a mossy stone.
Style: Genshin Impact.
reasoning:
Since the changes affect most of the module, I'll reply with the entire rewritten file rather than a diff. I'm working out the geometry constants first—stone surface height, lathe offsets, and reduced stone radius—before drafting the full module.

Now I'm scaling the stone and ground profiles down proportionally, recalculating the paw-to-body spine length to shrink the animal about 12%, and planning to sample the stone's dome-shaped top using a downward ray cast at each paw position to get accurate placement heights.

I'm also checking that all paws—hind, front, and the lifted one—stay within the stone's top radius given the new centered position, and confirming the tail is allowed to overhang past the ground's edge since it curves sideways off the platform.

Now I'm plotting the tail's path from the hips, arcing it rearward then sideways and upward so it's visible beside the head in the front view, adjusting the lateral offsets and tip height to get a natural sweeping curve.

To keep the silhouette clean I'm moving the crystal cluster to the opposite side from the tail, placing it near the hind leg within the ground circle so it doesn't overlap with the tail's visible arc.

Placing mushrooms and flowers on the +x front keeps things balanced across viewing angles. I'm scaling down the crystal heights to 60% of their originals and shrinking their radii proportionally, then adjusting the ground lathe profile to taper smoothly to the 0.47 max radius with a thin base edge.

I'm checking whether anything dips 48mm below ground level — rocks, stones, and the tail all seem fine at their offsets, so the culprit is probably the grass cards scattered via groundFrames selection logic.

I'm trying to figure out why the lowest point sits 48mm below y=0 even after accounting for card normals and hanging vines, but I can't pin down the exact source. Maybe I should just compute a precise bounding box after building and shift things to compensate rather than chasing the root cause.

Checking the crystal placements and tilt angles for minor dips below ground level, then wondering if the actual culprit is something at ground level itself — comparing BASE_H against where the lathe-based ground mesh actually starts.

Actually I think I found it: when new cards get placed by finding the nearest surface point on the root mesh, they might be landing on an existing card quad instead of the ground or stone, and if that card's normal points downward, the new card would offset by its own size in the wrong direction — explaining that suspicious -48mm displacement. The fix is to make sure surface lookups use the saved ground mesh specifically rather than the whole root, which includes all the card geometry already placed.

Now I'm working out the ground sampling and scatter logic — building a ground skin surface, filtering by upward-facing normals, and excluding the area already covered by the stone's footprint, while keeping a quiet mossy ring undisturbed near the animal. I'm also reconciling the coordinate offsets between the stone, ground, and panda centers so the visible ring of ground isn't accidentally too narrow once everything is aligned.

I'm checking whether the panda's head and nose overhang past the ground's front edge, and considering nudging the whole animal's position back slightly to keep it from clipping outside the ground circle.

Now I'm working through the tail position overhanging behind the ground, and starting to draft the spine path coordinates for the panda module, from hips through chest.

For the neck, I'm planning to raise the neck joint from 0.075 to 0.095 and shift it forward slightly, keeping the overall curve shape consistent with the original structure.

Now adjusting body proportions: shrinking the chest end z slightly, increasing vertical body radii by about 12%, and nudging the center offset down a touch. I'm also repositioning the haunch and shoulder blend spheres deeper into the body with adjusted scale values to make the silhouette read more naturally.

For the legs, I'm working out foot placement so each paw sits correctly on the stone surface — casting a ray down from each paw's x/z position to find the stone's top height, then setting the paw sphere's center so its bottom edge sinks just slightly (1-2mm) into that surface for a grounded contact look.

For toe spheres, I'm confirming their smaller scale keeps them tucked safely above the paw's bottom edge so they don't clip through.

Now I'm designing the makePaw function to accept a per-paw contact height, with support for a lifted paw that floats above the stone and rotates downward at the wrist to angle the toes, working through how X-axis rotation affects the paw's orientation in three.js space.

I'm working out which paw should appear lifted and visible in the three-quarter view, trying to determine the panda's orientation relative to the camera to decide which side is forward-facing.

Tracing through the geometry, I conclude the camera is seeing the model's +X side (head toward image-left matches this setup), so the left front paw (frontL) should be the one lifted, with frontR and hindL planted on the ground.

Now I'm checking whether the torso's center of mass actually falls within the support triangle formed by the three planted paws. Computing the triangle edges at the torso's z-position, the center x≈0 lands right at the boundary—essentially unsupported—so I likely need to shift the planted front paw's position inward to keep the pose balanced.

Now I'm checking the lifted paw's reach against the stone surface, verifying the leg segment lengths from shoulder to target foot position still sum correctly for the inverse kinematics to work, and computing the y-coordinate offset for the wrist target relative to the stone height.

I'm figuring out a floorAt helper that raycasts down onto the stone to get surface height at any x,z, falling back to FL when nothing's hit, making sure the stone's lathe geometry gives top heights close to FL=0.255 near center and tapering slightly at the edges.

I'm also making sure ray origins start above the stone so they hit the stone top first rather than grass cards, and planning to compute paw contact points early (reordering scatter logic before the body) so moss and grass can be excluded within 60mm of paw contacts.

Now I'm working out the exclusion radius around each paw center and reconsidering the stone's top radius so grass and moss lumps sit correctly along the rim without overlapping the paws.

I'm placing the rune decal at the stone surface, sizing it, then working out positions for small satellite rocks and crystals scattered around the ground ring.

Checking the remaining crystal positions confirms no overlap with the stone or panda silhouette, and I'm placing motes clustered near the crystals around x -0.42, y 0.15-0.3. Now I'm working out mushroom placement, making sure the front-right positioning matches the viewer's perspective correctly.

Checking the lifted paw doesn't overlap mushrooms, then placing flowers near front-left and adjusting satellite rock positions so none poke past the stone's edge radius.

Now adding pebbles in a loop around the ground, and plotting vine points hanging down the stone's sides at specific angles, making sure they stay clear of the chest area.

For the ground grass, I'm scattering roughly 17 cards onto the outer ring beyond the stone's footprint, avoiding buried overlaps, then planning a handful of flower cards to finish the scene.

Now I'm adjusting the moss palette, pulling the lit and shadow greens down about 20% from the original bright tones so the lumps on the stone surface read as darker, more muted moss rather than vivid grass green.

I'm shifting the body colors toward a richer red-russet family—a warm rust as the main tone, a lighter rust-orange for upper accents, a deeper burnt rust for the head, and a dark rust for cel-shaded areas—while keeping the belly a dark brownish tone. I'm also reworking the fur edge pattern along the belly boundary to use a larger, more deliberate scalloped shape instead of the dense near-black scallops from before.

Tuning leg coloring and coat...

Now I'm working out the tail shape — thickening near the base, swelling around the midpoint to its widest, then tapering to a rounded, slender tip using an eased radius function along its length.

For the tail rings, I'm planning 7 alternating bands of warm orange and deep russet, but making the very tip dark to match how real red panda tails end, with the rounded cap colored as a single solid dome rather than split across bands.

Now I'm shifting the tail fur to low-poly wedge shapes instead of flat tuft cards—thinking of a small squashed cone geometry function to scatter sparse 15-20mm fur wedges along the outer curve of the tail.

For orientation, since a basic cone is symmetric around its axis and can't lean back naturally, I'm considering how to skew or shear the geometry so the wedges tilt backward like real fur rather than sticking straight up, possibly using a tetrahedron or custom extrusion instead. I'm also working out the sizing math so protrusion height matches the intended 10-19mm depending on body location (tail versus shoulders/elbows).

Writing wedge geometry function...

I'm thinking about coloring the tail wedges using position-based painting instead of UV bands, so I avoid wedges crossing tail bands and keep the russet gradient aligned with the actual tail curve by computing each point's closest position along the tail path.

Since calling closestT per texel could be costly, I'm instead opting to compute the band once per wedge hit and assign flat colors (alternating orange and russet) rather than full cel shading paints, to keep the atlas cost down while still looking visually coherent under scene lighting.

I still need to figure out how many tail wedges to scatter — roughly 12 spread over 15–20mm along the outer curve — and determine which side counts as "outer" based on how the tail arcs in the x direction.

I'll refine the filter to n.x<-0.4 || n.y>0.75, using about 10 wedges with minDist 0.07, each oriented along the tail's tangent direction toward the tip so they lean naturally. Then I'll add a few more wedges near the shoulders/elbows on the body sides for additional fur detail.

For the elbows, I'll find the nearest surface point on each leg's elbow joint (offset slightly backward) to place small stick wedges there, angled with flow direction pointing down and back, matching the natural fur lean at the joint.

For the body, I'm settling on roughly 6 flank wedges, 4 elbow wedges, and 10 tail wedges, colored with the lighter rust cel shade on the upper body and the standard rust for legs.

Now I'm working out the cheek ruff — a shallow, three-lobed tuft on each side of the head, about 65mm tall and overlapping the skull by at least 15mm, built as an extruded, smoothed outline with lobes pointing downward and backward relative to the head's local coordinate frame.

Still writing the outline coordinates...

I'm tracing the path counter-clockwise to confirm no self-intersections, checking each lobe tip and valley point flows correctly into the next, and the overall height comes out to roughly 65-75mm, which looks reasonable.

Since the edges between adjacent points are short, I want to avoid smoothing causing cut corners to cross each other—I'll settle on smoothing level 1 with careful attention to valley spacing, since each edge's neighbors only get a quarter cut, keeping the total well under the full edge length.

Now I'm checking that the slab's placement overlaps the skull surface by at least 15mm, working through the skull's half-width at the given height and comparing it against the slab's x-span to confirm sufficient embedding depth.

I'm angling the tuft's extrude direction outward and backward rather than straight along the forward axis, so it slants naturally away from the skull instead of poking straight out.

Now I'm double-checking the skull's position and scale relative to the head joint — confirming its front surface sits around z 0.385 — and recalculating the muzzle's placement so it sits properly in front of the skull rather than overlapping it.

I'll obey the spec and keep forward at 0.13. For the nose, I'm pulling it back 25mm to sit properly on top of the muzzle's front surface, positioning it at forward 0.16, up 0.004, with a small scale so it rests naturally on the muzzle slope.

Now I'm working out the mouth points, draping them onto the muzzle surface with coordinates narrowing toward the front, then shifting to the lower jaw placement, anchoring it to the jaw bone further back and down from the head's local origin.

Whiskers get positioned sprouting from the muzzle sides, angling outward and slightly down toward the front. For the head markings, I'm setting up distance calculations from the head coat center to use for shading the cream muzzle patch and surrounding skull coat pattern.

Now I'm defining the broader cream cheek patches with a zigzag upper edge transitioning to rust above, covering the lower lateral face and jaw region, while leaving the hidden underside of the skull mostly unaddressed since it's not visible.

For tear markings, I'm working out the eye position on the skull using azimuth/elevation angles projected onto the ellipsoid surface, then placing a deeper brown stripe running downward and outward from each eye to mark the tear streaks.

Tapering the tear line width from 0.008 to 0.003, limiting it to the front face, and using a darker brown "#6e2a18" so it reads distinctly against the rust-orange head and shows up well against the cream patch. I'll skip adding a lighter forehead accent stripe to keep things simple.

Now I'm shrinking the white brow marks into shallow, flat cream-colored markings instead of full spheres—scaling the sphere geometry thin along the normal axis so each mark sits close to the surface above each eye, roughly at elevation 38 with a flattened scale.

For the eyelid, I'm considering a thin arc-shaped sweep or decal placed just above the eye to suggest an upper lid, using a rust-colored shape with a dark line rather than true 3D geometry, sized small and layered over the eye decal.

Writing lid SVG code... I'm also noting the lid will need to cover the brow and lash details already drawn in the eye texture, so I should check that the fill overlaps those strokes correctly.

I worry the lid covers too much of the brow and lash flicks, so I'm shrinking its coverage to keep the lashes visible. But I'm also concerned about color mismatch between the flat decal fill and the cel-shaded paint under standard lighting, so I'm considering dropping the filled lid entirely in favor of just a thick ink arc along the top edge, maybe paired with a dark teal fill instead.

Settling on a hooded half-lid look: a thin crescent shape filled with dark rust brown, outlined with a thick ink line along the curve.

Writing SVG path code...

I'll place this decal above the eye, layered after the eye decal with a slightly bigger surface lift so the lid sits above the eye texture on the skull's skin, with no mirroring needed since the lid is symmetrical.

Checking eye placement with azimuth around 36 degrees keeps the eyes readable from the front on the broad skull, and I'm confirming the direction vector and resulting offsets match the tear-start coordinates I set earlier for consistency. Moving on to work out the ears next.

I'm shaping the ears as shallow rounded triangular forms embedded into the skull, defining the outline dimensions, smoothing, thickness, and bevel, then working out which way the extrusion plane should face so the ears point forward-outward correctly.

Now I'm figuring out the ear's position, placing it at the top corner of the skull using the skull's elliptical curvature to find the right coordinates.

I realize the ear base, being horizontal, floats about 27mm above the sloped skull surface at its outer corner, creating a gap. I need to tilt the ear's base orientation to follow the skull's outward slope instead, adjusting the x-axis direction so the base corner sits flush against the surface rather than hovering above it.

Working out the correct normal direction for each side so the ear faces outward properly instead of flipping backward for the mirrored side...

Confirming the normal points forward, giving the ear an outward tilt of about 29° so it reads as a rounded triangular panda ear. Now I'm working out where to anchor the ear base on the skull surface, computing the local offsets for side, height, and forward position relative to the head center.

I'm checking whether the ear base would actually sit buried inside the skull dome at that location, comparing the dome's height just behind versus just in front of the ear plane to see if the geometry clashes.

Since the skull rises forward and covers the ear's front edge, I think tilting the ear slightly back works fine naturally—that's just how ears sit on top-back of a head, roughly 80mm wide by 85mm tall and positioned on the outer sides.

Now I'm planning the ear coloring: a rust-brown outer ear with the characteristic white rim and cream inner shape that red pandas have.

I'm settling on cream as the main ear body with a smaller rust-orange inset on the front face, so the cream rim reads as "white-edged" while still showing warm color inside, matching how red panda ears actually look with pale rims and darker interior fur.

Still computing inset geometry...

Now I'm checking other requirements: the ear embedded 15-20mm into the skull with the base centered 18mm below the surface, confirming ear spikes are removed and nothing's blocking the front of the face. For the skull I'm setting the scale and verifying the rear of the head connects cleanly to the neck joint and tube radius tapering from .078 to .07, then narrowing the scarf's radius to 0.018.

Now I'm working out the gold edging along the scarf boundaries, placing thin sweeps near the scarf loop offset along the neck's tangent direction so they hug the band properly, using frame-based positioning to keep the offsets aligned with the neck axis rather than defaulting to world-up.

I'm checking whether the scarf loop plane, perpendicular to the tilted neck direction, might accidentally intersect the chest or shoulder geometry rather than cleanly wrapping the neck tube, comparing the neck radius profile against nearby body sphere extents at that height.

For the scarf's stripe pattern, I'm using the loop parameter to alternate stripes along the sweep, keeping that logic as-is. For the knot and tails, I want the pendant placed just ahead of the scarf tails so the emblem is fully visible, with tails short enough to clear the lifted foreleg and draped in a soft fold rather than looking like rigid rectangles -- currently positioning the knot at a lower-front point on the neck surface, with tails originally offset slightly to either side.

Writing tail extrude geometry...

I'm working out the x-axis perpendicular direction for the extrusion and applying a gold paint threshold near the hem at the bottom of the outline. I also need to check that the hanging tails clear the lifted foreleg, and I'm estimating the neck-front position relative to the shoulder and radius.

Now I'm tracing where the tails attach near the neck's forward-down elevation point, then following them down to see if they end up floating in front of the chest rather than resting against it—checking whether that gap looks wrong in the render.

Recalculating the chest surface geometry — the body's rounded end cap actually extends the front surface out to z≈0.22 at the chest height, so the tails should hug that surface closer to z≈0.208 rather than floating in front of it.

Rather than chase exact surface math, it's simpler to offset the tail origin by a small fixed amount (about 0.012) outward from the neck/chest hit point, giving the tails thickness 0.008 and anchoring them at the knot position plus a small z offset so they sit naturally against the chest.

I'm checking that the tails stay clear of the lifted leg geometry near the shoulder, confirming the x-offsets keep enough clearance. Then for the pendant, I'll dangle it from a tiny chain at chest center, positioned slightly in front of the tails (greater z) and lower (negative y offset) so the emblem faces forward and is fully visible.

I'm setting the tails plane at the knot's z position, with the pendant offset forward by about 0.016-0.021 to sit slightly off the chest like it's hanging from a chain, adding a thin rod connecting the knot to the disc. Now I need to pin down the knot's exact position, tracing it back to the neck surface point at elevation -40 degrees, being careful since the neck tube's radius might place that point inside the chest surface rather than on it.

Checking the numbers confirms the knot sits about 0.02 inside the chest body, which means I need a different approach -- casting a ray against the body skin itself from a point in front of the chest and finding where it intersects, rather than relying on the neck surface calculation.

Checking the scarf loop around the neck — part of it sits buried inside the chest geometry since the neck tube dips into the body front at that angle, but the top and sides should still peek out as the visible teal band, matching the original render.

Rather than guessing at a fixed knot position, I realize it's cleaner to place the knot directly on the scarf's loop path itself, sampling the loop at a given parameter so it naturally sits where the front-lower part of the neck loop falls.

That point sits right near the chest surface, so the bottom of the loop may actually get buried in the body geometry — matching how the old render shows the scarf as a V-shape with tails hanging from a knot in front. I'll just place the knot at that computed front position with a visible sphere, let the tails hang from there with the pendant in front, and not worry about the arc dipping slightly into the chest since the raised neck should keep it mostly clear.

Given the ambiguity, I'll just settle on a practical compromise: place the scarf around the neck at t=0.4, derive the knot position via a ray cast toward the chest front at roughly body-center height, and let the tails extrude from there. The body tube and neck mesh basically merge in that region anyway, so exact precision isn't critical as long as it reads visually correct from the front.

Checking the geometry confirms both neck and chest surfaces meet around z≈0.22 at that height, so the knot sits right at that junction. The tails then hang down from the knot point along the chest front, with z receding slightly from 0.22 to about 0.19 as y drops.

The scarf loop near t=0.4 also lines up with the knot, with its bottom edge sinking into the chest mass - that's fine since the knot sphere covers that area anyway. I'm placing the pendant just below and in front of the knot, connected by a small rod, then moving on to the tail wedges and glow intensities: crystals at 0.7/1.0 (core/tip), motes at full strength, and no glow on the rune.

I'm dialing back emissive strength on mushrooms, dots, the flower heart, and emblem so nothing visually competes for attention, while also softening the crystal base and tip colors slightly. I'm checking that the floor stone sits properly inset into the ground mesh, confirming the loose octahedron motes are still part of the scene, and now working through a tilt calculation for the crystal cylinders to make sure their base rim doesn't clip below the floor.

Now I'm figuring out paw placement for the hind legs, defining the paw center and wrist heights relative to floor height so they land naturally, and adjusting the hind foot's z-offset for correct stance positioning.

For the hind hip, I'm checking the geometry: from hip joint to foot, computing the leg segment lengths and verifying the knee bends forward correctly for a short, sturdy hind leg shape.

Now for the front legs, I'm working out shoulder position and foot placement separately for the planted leg versus the lifted leg, with the elbow bending backward. For the lifted paw, I'm tilting the wrist slightly downward and computing the hover height above the floor using the floor height function plus a clearance offset.

Verifying lift height comes out to roughly 37mm (within the 35-40mm target) and forward reach to 50mm matches spec. Now I'm defining the four paw target positions (hindL, hindR, frontR, frontL) with their x/z coordinates and lift offsets for the gait.

Writing paw geometry function...

Now I'm working through the rig hierarchy, keeping the original joint naming convention for hips and chains, and checking the jaw aim setup and cheek ruff colors. I'm also verifying the cheek positioning logic with signed offsets before moving to scattering wedge tufts across the body surface for the shoulders.

For the wedge scatter, I'm confirming the filter and spacing produce the right depth (around 8-12mm) at shoulder and elbow regions, using rust-light coloring for the upper-facing stick tufts, and checking that the stick function correctly accepts flat and flow parameters alongside the hit normal and position data.

For the stone, I'll keep the lathe at 9 segments rather than bumping to 10, and verify the ground mesh returned by the lathe function works properly with the surface skin for scattering. I'm setting ground card sizes and confirming the top surface normal threshold for placing ground scatter, then deciding to strip out the tuft texture cards for cheek fur entirely, possibly keeping a small chin tuft.

Now I'm checking the eye decal placement using the raycast hit point, deciding to skip extra forehead stripe marks, and confirming the brow shape as a flattened sphere. For the tail, I'm verifying the paint banding count and joint chain spans match the path point count, then checking the tail path coordinates near the base and tip to make sure they align with the body geometry.

Checking the tail's reach in front view confirms it rises high enough to sit beside the head, with its tip extending past the body's width near the ear height. I'm also verifying the tail clears the hips and ground properly, then settling on the color palette for the tail rings—a deep russet paired with an orange tone.

Finalizing the color constants now: a rust base, lighter rust highlight, head rust, dark rust, plus belly, paw, toe, cream, cream shadow, and tear-stain tones. With those locked in, I'm defining the body's fur edge shading using the rust and belly tones with specific teeth and period parameters for the fur texture.

The belly boundary should zigzag with large scallops along the body length, giving a few bigger shaped transitions rather than tight fur teeth — roughly 2.5 scallops across the torso. I'm making sure the fur coat function uses world-space z-position so shading stays continuous across the shoulder and haunch spheres, avoiding seams between body parts. Now I'm setting up the leg coat shading using the same position-based fur edge approach.

Now I'm coding the tear-mark detail on the head paint function, computing a tapered line segment distance for the teardrop streak near the eye.

I'm checking the geometry: the eye decal sits at dx=0.058, dy=0.007, with the tear starting right at the eye's bottom edge and extending outward. But I need to verify the skull's ellipsoid surface actually exists at that point—computing dx²/a²+dy²/b² shows it exceeds 1 at the tear's endpoint, meaning that location falls outside the skull surface entirely.

I'm adjusting the tear's endpoint to a valid point on the ellipsoid, testing (0.085, -0.062) which satisfies the surface constraint and gives a usable dz value.

Now I'm working out where the cream cheek patches should sit relative to the tear mark, defining conditions based on dx and dy so the cream appears broadly on the cheek area while leaving room for a small cream patch near the muzzle region.

Writing zigzag boundary logic...

I'm keeping a subtle lighter stripe at mid-forehead and shallow cream markings for eyebrow dots, with cream undersides below dy -0.065. For the muzzle, I'm sizing a broad part and adding a dark nose plus inner mouth lines, confirming the cheek ruff and muzzle stay separate from the skull decals while ears attach via head.local positioning.

Now I'm writing a helper to exclude areas near paws from stone scatter, then filtering ground stone and grass placement by surface normal and radius ranges, adjusting grass counts based on stone size.

Checking the front paw position against the stone radius confirms it fits within the moss ring. I verify the head and nose stay clear of the stone's front edge and ground boundary, hovering safely above. The rune decal targets the stone's front face along the Z direction, and I'm considering whether the 9-gon lathe's spin puts a vertex or edge facing forward where the decal projects.

I check the flower position against its radial distance from center, confirming it clears the main group, then scatter grass cards across the ground using a radial filter that keeps them within a ring band around the stone while avoiding overlap with mushrooms.

I'm scattering a few flower cards too, checking that the ground's filter excludes spots buried under the stone, and confirming the tail wedge geometry and vine path callback still work fine as originally written. Then I move on to placing motes around the crystal cluster.

I set up the crystal helper function with glowing bodies and tips, keep the original mushroom scattering with glowing caps and dots, and verify that the decal and lathe glow functions return proper parts. I'm also trimming the crystal dimensions down and starting to look at the eye lid detail.

For the lid decal, I'm positioning it above the eye center but realize my initial height leaves the top brow strokes uncovered, so I'm adjusting the lid height and center position to properly span the eye region, accounting for the source image's aspect ratio.

Adjusting the eye decal size to better fit the broader head proportions, then recalculating the lid dimensions to match—now moving on to the scarf details, setting up a sweep radius and lift value using a point along the neck curve for the loop placement.

For the gold edging, I'm using offset points along the neck tangent to create loop cross-sections above and below center, sweeping thin gold tubes through them with a small radius and pentagon profile. I'm confirming the tube weighting follows the same approach as before, then moving to define the tails, starting by raycasting against the body and neck surfaces to find a reference point with a fallback in case the ray misses.

Now I'm adding a knot sphere embedded at that point and generating two symmetric tail pieces, each defined by a sequence of direction vectors and offset points that curve outward and downward from the knot before being extruded into tube geometry.

Since x and y aren't strictly perpendicular, I need a helper to compute a proper perpendicular x-direction before taking the cross product for thickness, though since the extrusion is a closed solid the exact orthogonality may not matter visually. I'll paint gold trim on the hem where the piece's y-coordinate drops below a threshold, marking the narrow gold edging near the scarf's tail.

Now I'm positioning the pendant: placing it just below and in front of the knot, modeling it as a thin disc with an emblem circle on its face, then adding a connecting rod from the knot down to the top of the pendant to represent the chain.

Setting glow to 0.7 and assigning rust-light accent color to ear outsides and wedge shapes. I'm writing a helper that builds a wedge shape from a cone geometry, skewing the top vertices backward and scaling it to a flattened, elongated form.

Now I'm scattering points along the tail tube surface to place tail wedges, filtering by position and normal direction so they land toward the back and outer sides.

Checking that tail band coloring and elbow wedge placement use consistent coordinate math—verifying the tube band calculation and nearest-point lookup for the elbow joint position.

Planning wedge placement: sticking a rust-colored wedge at the elbow with embed and flow parameters, limiting to front legs only plus shoulder wedges. For the body, I'm scattering wedges across the shoulder region filtered by height and normal direction, then adding haunch wedges with a different z-filter, combining both sets.

Switching to body scatter parameters and wedge coloring, confirming bones and surface sweep work correctly. I still need cheek ruff placement — extruding the cheek geometry at an offset position on the head, with thickness and direction mirrored per side.

Checking the thickness axis math confirms the normal points consistently outward regardless of side, and the cheek placement lines up against the skull's forward and vertical offsets.

Calculating the ruff's position relative to the head center, I'm finding the lobe tips extend well beyond the skull's narrower cross-section at that height, meaning the ruff geometry floats outside the skull surface rather than embedding into it as intended.

I should tilt the ruff plane so its normal angles inward toward the bottom, letting the top sit flush against the cheek while the lower tips pull in closer to match the skull's taper, rather than treating it as a flat vertical plate.

Realizing my tilted axis isn't orthogonal, I'm writing a small helper to orthonormalize the direction vectors so the ruff plane's x and y axes stay perpendicular, then applying it to compute proper tilted coordinates for both the ruff and tails.

Checking the placement, the ruff tips land just outside the skull at the overlap point, and the top edge stays fully buried under the skull's curvature by over 15mm, confirming good coverage. I run similar checks on the ears and front-view markings, and both look fine, with the jaw and mouth needing to sit on the jaw bone and the eyes/mouth needing reprojection onto the revised surfaces -- all consistent. Now I'm moving on to the paw function.

Verifying the leg coat lifts correctly and that the root structure returns properly, then confirming import order between the stone surface and skin functions so legs build after the floor is available. I'm also double-checking the limb, catmull, rng, paint, noise, cells, and svg imports are all correctly pulled in, along with furEdge and zigzag for the body coat, and confirming INK is used appropriately before computing ear and body heights from the leg length.

Now I'm working out the ear geometry — computing direction vectors for the ear's local axes, placing the base point relative to the head joint, and extruding the ear shape with cream coloring and bevel smoothing, with a rust-colored inset planned for the rim detail.

Computing the ear base position against the skull curve, I'm checking whether the outer corner of the ear actually lands on the skull surface at that depth, and finding the geometry doesn't quite work since the square root term goes negative there.

Checking the center point, the embedding is too deep, so I raise the ear base position; then verifying the outer corner sticks out slightly and the inner corner embeds properly at 18mm, which looks right. I'm positioning the ear base relative to the head's local coordinates.

Positioning the ear further forward means its thickness faces outward with the back hidden against the skull, consistent with how panda ears typically sit; the skull dome in front covers the ear's lower embedded region, which works. Now checking the ear height extending above the skull at the tip point.

I'm setting up the inner ear inset extrusion using local coordinates relative to the ear frame, then moving on to whiskers, confirming that extrude accepts Vector3 directions, adjusting the ground lathe segment count, and finalizing the module with its imports.

Now I'm defining the spine chain with hip joint direction and start point, naming three spine segments between four control points, and configuring a two-span neck chain from base to end. I also write a helper function that raycasts downward from a given x,z position to find the floor height, then begin specifying the paw placement configuration for each limb.

Writing paw positions...

Contact only matters for the planted leg role, so I'll leave it optional for the front "arm" legs. I still need a perpTo helper function, and I should note the body wedge scatter depends on bodySkin being defined after the body itself — so my code order should be base joints, scenery, body, legs, tail, head, then scarf.
